title: Prophecy, Scorn and a Rejection of This World: The Forbidding Vision of a Faith-Healing Preacher
author: Noelle Crombie
content:
It was a stark and forbidding vision for those who followed the righteous
path. Scorn, the preacher told his congregation, was a person’s lot if they
led an “honest, clean, pure, godly life.” The world hated “people that live
like that,” he said.

“They want you to be just as ungodly and filthy as they are,” he said in a
rare audio recording, obtained by The Oregonian/OregonLive, of a 1958 sermon.

The preacher was Walter White, who led an Oregon City offshoot of the
Followers of Christ, an Idaho sect that spurns medical treatment as a show of
faith. White was a grocer, originally from Picabo, Idaho, whose congregants
came to view as a prophet. He rambled at times during his sermon but always
returned to simple and severe messages about choosing righteousness rather
than the ways of the world. A trim figure in wire-rim glasses and dark combed-
back hair, he spoke in a voice that evoked the stentorian tones of an old
newsreel announcer. In the scratchy recording, people cough and babies cry as
he preaches.

White was uneasy about being taped, according to a note by the congregant who
made the recording. White didn’t want his message to fall into what he thought
were undesirable hands. He viewed disbelievers with disgust. They put their
trust in human experts, such as doctors, rather than in God. People like that,
he told the faithful, “want to be somebody.” They want “the wisdom of the
world and admiration.”

Today, nearly 60 years after White’s death, his pronouncements continue to
influence the faithful. For many Followers, White remained “the highest
authority,” said Mark Shaw, who left the sect in 2019 and keeps in touch with
some Followers. Members invoked his teachings to settle disagreements. “It was
used as the trump card,” he said. “It was the discussion-ender.”

![A flat gravestone with the words “Our Minister Walter White” and the years
1902 and 1969.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Walter-
White3273_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)White’s
grave in the Followers’ cemetery outside of Oregon City Beth Nakamura/The
Oregonian

To understand the modern-day Oregon City congregation, it’s essential to
examine White’s role. No pastor ever succeeded him, leaving the sect all the
more reliant on his teachings.

The Oregonian/OregonLive and ProPublica have published a series of articles in
recent months about the Followers of Christ in Oregon and
[Idaho](https://www.propublica.org/article/idaho-law-faith-healing-exemption),
focusing on the long history of parents in Followers congregations [declining
to seek medical care](https://www.propublica.org/article/faith-healing-idaho-
deaths-followers-of-christ) for their critically ill children and the
[sometimes fatal consequences](https://www.propublica.org/article/idaho-faith-
healing-multiple-deaths).

Little has been publicly known about White, likely due to the Followers’
culture of isolation and secrecy. The Oregonian/OregonLive was able to piece
together details through documents we obtained, including biographical
sketches, a transcript and the recording of the sermon, along with written
accounts of dreams White purported to have and records of baptisms he
performed. Among the documents was a list of his prophecies and even a sex
guide he disseminated.

White was born into the Followers, whose members migrated to Idaho from the
Midwest around the turn of the 20th century. Men in White’s family preached,
and he joined them in his 20s, the story goes, after he dreamed that worms
would devour him if he didn’t.

In the early 1930s, White joined two church elders on a journey from Idaho to
Oregon City to minister to a dying man. After talking with them, the man
readily discarded his medications and was relieved to see White, an avid
smoker, roll a cigarette because the man didn’t want to kick the habit. For
the next five years, White traveled between Idaho and Oregon to preach and by
1938, he had moved to Oregon to lead a fledgling congregation.

Followers at the time were led by a constellation of preachers and elders, all
men. Notes from one of their meetings in 1937 revealed that Followers believed
White possessed the “gift of prophecy.” It also recorded the debates that
simmered among them — whether women should be allowed to cut their hair, for
instance. They talked about the value of dictionaries, which some classified
as “worldly” items to be avoided, and determined that women assisting with
home births should not “look under the cover” as women labored. One account
written years later by a Follower suggested that White split with a prominent
Idaho preacher after revelations that the man had sexual contact with a
15-year-old girl.

Some of those values still shape the Followers today. Congregants tend to stay
out of what they view as the worldly affairs of politics and civic life, and
they generally don’t pursue education beyond high school or vocational
training. The Followers remain patriarchal; men are expected to lead their
households.

![A black-and-white photo of a group of suited men standing and kneeling
outside of a large house.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/Walter-White-Followers-of-Christ-
Oregon2500_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)White,
second from left in the back (in suspenders), with Followers leaders in Oregon
City in 1937. By 1938, he had moved to Oregon to lead a fledgling
congregation. Courtesy of the Phillips family

White was known among Followers as “brother Walter.” An undated black-and-
white photograph shows him baptizing a child in what appears to be a baptismal
pool, his arm raised in prayer. In another image dated 1951, he wears a suit
jacket and tie, a mug in one hand and a cigarette in the other.

As much a ruler as a spiritual leader, White enjoyed near-absolute authority.
Followers believed he possessed such divine power that he knew their thoughts
and secrets. They turned to him for approval on matters both consequential and
mundane, from marital advice to appliance purchases. (White even weighed in on
where to shop: He owned a local market and made it clear he expected to see
Followers there.)

White’s earthly teachings extended to a perhaps unexpected realm: Couples on
the cusp of marriage received a sex guide, which continued to be distributed
as recently as 2018. Complete with explicit detail and anatomical diagrams,
the 15-page manual includes chapters titled “the ideal love act” and “the
control of climax.” And, in a seeming exception to the prohibition on medical
treatment, it goes so far as to recommend that women who feel inhibited should
consider seeing a doctor “who has given the sex problems sincere study.”

* * *

White preached the Oregon City sect’s singularity: His flock was spiritually
superior to other Follower congregations, he contended, including ones in
Idaho and Grants Pass, Oregon. By the 1950s, he had cut off ties to those
groups.

In 1965, White told his congregation of his prophecy that the end times were
near. He recounted a dream, which he said was set against the backdrop of the
Kennedy Space Center in Florida, that involved walking with Jesus Christ,
according to one account. He dreamed they climbed a launchpad, and White noted
he was impressed with Christ’s physical agility. Days before White shared his
vision, NASA launched Gemini 3, the first U.S. mission to send multiple
astronauts into space.

White told the faithful that it was during this dream that Christ said the
world would come to an end in six years. He said Christ warned that baptisms
among the Followers would end even sooner. That his apocalyptic prophecy
fizzled didn’t shake Followers’ faith.

White died in 1969. He was seen as irreplaceable. A handful of elders divided
his leadership duties but lacked White’s authority. The faithful never tapped
a successor, believing only a man called by God could fill the role. No one
was ever deemed worthy enough to take his place.

But one element of White’s prophecy did come true. Given that he was the only
person who could perform baptisms, his passing also meant that the ritual
ended. As a result, the flock, which former members say numbered 1,500 or more
at its peak, today consists solely of generations of the same families who
were members in 1969.

* * *

Like other elders in the early days of the Followers, White saw illness as a
test of faith. During the 1937 meeting, about 18 elders and preachers from
congregations in Idaho and Oregon gathered at the Oregon City meetinghouse to
settle the rules that would shape the church, according to a written account
compiled by sect members years later.

The men discussed the Book of James in the New Testament, which says, “And the
prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up.”
Followers interpret the lines as an edict to rely only on faith when faced
with illness. The passage would be “strictly enforced to show faith,”
according to an account of the meeting compiled years later. They believed
that death, if it came, was God’s will.

![A black-and-white photo with a frilly white edge. A group of men are eating
and laughing together, sitting on wooden pews and
chairs.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Followers-of-
Christ3058-no-bkg-sm.png?w=1149)White with other Followers. He preached that
the Oregon City congregation was spiritually superior to other Followers
congregations. Courtesy of the Phillips family

Years later, in 1965, when the state investigated the case of a teen in the
sect whose broken ankle had gone untreated, White said, “faith can heal,”
according to a story in The Oregonian at the time. “We believe that God comes
before man. If a person’s faith doesn’t go far enough, then he can seek help
from man.”

The consequences of this belief system still reverberate. For years, the
Oregon City Followers suffered multiple child deaths, many from treatable or
preventable conditions. The deaths prompted the Legislature in 1999 to chip
away at legal protections for parents whose children died without medical
care. Then in 2011, lawmakers removed all protections for faith healing.

The faith-healing doctrine would affect White’s own descendants. Two of his
great-granddaughters spent years in prison for failing to seek medical care
for their premature newborns who died. In 2017, one of his great-great-
granddaughters, Evelyn, suffered respiratory complications related to her
premature birth. Authorities attribute her survival to the intervention of law
enforcement officials who ordered her parents to get her to the hospital.
Evelyn’s life and journey out of the Followers is the subject of a
[story](https://www.propublica.org/article/followers-of-christ-oregon-city-
evelyn-marshall-phillips) and
[documentary](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kM6Ewe9rkGc) published by The
Oregonian/OregonLive and ProPublica.
